They now join at a few points, which keeps the forces simpler and the construction affordable. The facade can be opened for natural ventilation. Each use is gathered in its own block, yet the different groups of users cross paths at many points inside, an idea OMA calls a vertical city.

Tore Björnstad's Maison de Radio-Canada in Montréal was the broadcast headquarters of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's French-language radio and television, with its studios and master control. Most of the working-class Faubourg à m'lasse neighbourhood had to be demolished to build it, and the last house was evacuated on 1 October 1963 so that demolition could go ahead. The old complex's address is 1400 René Lévesque Boulevard East, a street named after the former premier who was once a CBC reporter and commentator. A new building at 1000 Papineau Avenue was inaugurated on 7 September 2022. By April 2025 most of the old buildings had been demolished for a future residential project, and the new development would relink the street grid through the site.

On Manhattan's Upper East Side, at 200 East 66th Street, Manhattan House rises 21 storeys. New York Life developed it between 1949 and 1951 as middle-class housing, and Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed it with Mayer & Whittlesey. A central spine carries five wings that face north and south, and the block stands back from the streets on both its north and south sides. Older apartment houses in the city were different: their fronts ran right to the lot line, with gardens tucked inside. Manhattan House was one of New York's first buildings faced mainly in pale white brick. The brick was glazed, so rain carried the dirt away, and many later white-brick buildings in the city followed its lead. Stern saw it as the city's most literal take on Le Corbusier's postwar idea of vertical living.

Louis Kahn built nine houses, and this one in Philadelphia, finished in 1961, is among the most studied. Its client was Margaret Esherick, who owned a bookshop in Chestnut Hill. It has one bedroom in 2,500 square feet and reads as a flat-roofed rectangular block, its long face to the street, built of concrete block faced with stucco. Kahn liked to divide buildings into served and servant spaces; here four two-storey strips of the two kinds alternate, each crossing the house from front to back. Built-in bookshelves cover most of the front wall, and the copper and wood kitchen is the work of her uncle, the craftsman Wharton Esherick. No two sides share the same pattern of windows and ventilation. Beside each pair of large windows, two-storey stacks of shutters open in any mix, linking inside and out.

No skyscraper in Uruguay is taller than the Antel Tower, which stands 157 metres high with 35 floors on the edge of the Bay of Montevideo. ANTEL, the state-owned telecommunications company, has its headquarters inside. The design came from Carlos Ott, a Uruguayan-Canadian architect, and the building was finished in 2002 by American Bridge together with the other members of a design/build consortium. Officially it is the Torre de las Telecomunicaciones, and some know it as the Torre Joaquín Torres García. The tower is the centrepiece of a complex covering 19,459 square metres in total, alongside a Customer Service Building, a Telecommunications Museum and an Auditorium. Construction ran into problems, and the budget grew from $65 million at the outset to $102 million.

On the Japanese island of Naoshima, Benesse House is both an art museum and a hotel, designed by Tadao Ando. The idea took shape in 1985 between Tetsuhiko Fukutake, founding president of Fukutake Publishing, and Naoshima's mayor, Chikatsugu Miyake. When it opened in 1992 it was an early step in turning the island into a haven for art. Facing the mountains of Shikoku, it is arranged in four hotel areas, named Museum, Park, Beach and Oval. Art continues outside, where Yayoi Kusama's pumpkin sits at the water's edge. Ando returned in 2022 with two new galleries: the Valley Gallery, between Benesse House and the Chichu Art Museum, and the Hiroshi Sugimoto Gallery, which extends the Park. In 2025 Travel + Leisure counted it among the first art hotels in the world.

Frank Lloyd Wright designed only one Jewish house of worship: the main building of Beth Sholom in Elkins Park, finished in 1959. Rabbi Cohen turned down the International Style, then dominant, as too simple, since he wanted the building to say plainly that it was a synagogue. With his consent, Wright swapped an octagonal plan for a hexagon, and in February 1954 presented a scheme loosely based on Mount Sinai. A six-sided base of glass, steel and concrete carries a roof shaped as a tetrahedron. Each roof panel has corrugated plastic inside and wire glass outside; the two layers cut glare, eased summer ventilation and helped absorb heat in winter. The sanctuary has no columns, aisles, spires or traditional pews, and its floor falls towards the middle. Wright had died by the dedication on 20 September 1959.

Beside Exarcheia Square in Athens, where Arachovis and Themistokleous streets meet, the Blue Condominium is a block of flats regarded as a very important example of the city's modern architecture. The architect Kyriakos Panagiotakos designed it, and it was built for him in 1932–1933. Its name recalls the original colour of the facade, a deep blue picked by the painter Spyros Papaloukas. What looks like one block is really two separate six-floor buildings that meet at the top floor. The shared parts got special attention in both design and building: two entrance halls, concierge desks, corridors, stairs, a laundry, and a meeting room up on the top floor. The first plans also had a pool, but it was never completed. Le Corbusier came to see it while attending the fourth CIAM congress and called it very beautiful.

Built in 1964–66 as the Whitney Museum of American Art's third home, the Breuer Building in New York was later used by the Met, then by the Frick Collection, and now houses the headquarters of Sotheby's. Marcel Breuer led the design with Hamilton P. Smith. It was Breuer's first museum, and his first and only surviving work in Manhattan. Hard, angular shapes are clad in mixed-tone granite and bare concrete. Each upper floor reaches further over the entrance than the one below, like a ziggurat turned upside down, so the projecting front acts as a portico. Breuer picked materials that would weather and show their age: rough granite, slate floors laid split, teak, and bronze for the doors and fittings. The building shaped later projects, including Atlanta's Central Library and the north wing of the Cleveland Museum of Art.

The Church of the Light in Ibaraki, Osaka Prefecture, was built in 1989 and is one of Tadao Ando's most famous designs. It was planned as an addition to a wooden chapel and a minister's house already on the site. The building is a concrete volume of three 5.9-metre cubes, 17.7 metres long in all, cut through by a wall set at 15 degrees that separates the chapel from the entrance area. Behind the altar, a cross is cut into the concrete wall, running floor to ceiling and wall to wall and lined up with the joints of the concrete; daylight enters the chapel through it. The benches and floorboards are made from re-purposed scaffolding used in the construction. Ando often draws on Zen philosophies, and one theme he expresses here is the dual nature of existence.

Inaugurated in 1966 at 200 Avenida Ipiranga in central São Paulo, the Copan Building is a block of homes that Oscar Niemeyer designed to mark the city's fourth centenary. The engineer Joaquim Cardozo worked out the structure, while the curving facade was Niemeyer's own personal work. The aim was a building that a broad mix of Brazilians could share. Six blocks contain 1,160 apartments, home to an estimated five thousand people, along with over seventy shops and businesses. A hotel was planned as a second building, but only the housing went up. Copan stands for the first developer, Companhia Pan-Americana de Hotéis e Turismo. Rising 115 metres over 32 floors, it has Brazil's largest reinforced concrete structure. A see-through drape has wrapped it since 2014, shielding people on the street from mosaic tiles that come loose.

Parque Biblioteca Belén, known in English as Belén Library Park, sits in Comuna 16 and is one of ten library parks across Medellín, Colombia. The design came about through a university exchange. From 2006, Colombian universities ran a sharing programme with the University of Tokyo, and through it a team of Tokyo architects led by the Japanese architect Hiroshi Naito gave the library's design as a donation. Naito worked on the building together with the university, and it dates from 2008. Outside, the park offers three kinds of public space, each with its own mood: a green plaza, a plaza with water, and one left open for public use.

In Noisy-le-Grand, some 12 km from Paris, Les Espaces d'Abraxas packs housing at high density. Ricardo Bofill and his firm, Ricardo Bofill Taller de Arquitectura, drew it up in 1978 for the French state. Finished in 1982, it has 591 flats across three buildings: Le Palacio, the biggest; Le Théâtre on its west side; and L'Arc, a smaller block between the two. Its postmodern design uses classical motifs and new construction methods to reach a luxurious look once kept for the upper classes. The walls are precast concrete panels, coloured in several tones by adding oxides to the cement. All three buildings enclose a grassy plaza modelled on the forums of ancient Rome. Bofill saw that shared space as central, since he wanted the estate to 'mix social categories' and build a sense of community.

Hôtel van Eetvelde is a town house in Brussels that Victor Horta designed in Art Nouveau style for Edmond van Eetvelde, administrator of the Congo Free State. It was built between 1895 and 1898, and Horta added two extensions between 1898 and 1901. Its openly displayed steel and glass, materials then seen as industrial, were a novelty in prestigious private homes, and the facade uses a hanging steel construction. Inside, the plan of the central building turns around an octagonal rotunda topped by a skylight, and a reception room at the centre, under a stained glass cupola, brings extra light into the house. The rotunda works as a small winter garden, ringed by circulation that links the living room, dining room and stairwell. In 2000 it joined three other Horta town houses on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

Radio France has its headquarters in the Maison de la Radio in Paris, nicknamed the maison ronde, the round house. Henry Bernard won the commission against 26 competitors, and the building was finished in 1963. A vast ring measuring 500 metres around, with a service tower at its core, it holds the offices, studios and concert spaces for all of Radio France's national channels and its four standing ensembles. The land had been a gasworks and later a stadium, and it was thought perfect because the Eiffel Tower, with its radio transmitters, stood nearby. Architecture-Studio won a contract in October 2005. Faceted birch, beech and cherry panels line the walls and balcony fronts, and one 852-seat space has been known for excellent sound since 1963. A 1965 film used the building when such modernist designs still looked new and strange.

Sverre Fehn was the architect of the Norwegian Glacier Museum, known in Norwegian as Norsk Bremuseum, a building from 1991 at Fjærland in Norway's Vestland county. Its mission, in its own words, is to 'collect, create and disseminate knowledge about glaciers and climate'. Visitors can learn here about the Jostedalsbreen glacier and the national park that bears its name. Fehn's work on the museum went on in later years. In 2002 the museum chose to add an extension, and he designed that as well. A further addition by Fehn, the Ulltveit-Moe Climate Centre, opened as part of the museum in 2007.

Set behind the American Italian Cultural Center in downtown New Orleans, the Piazza d'Italia is a public square finished in 1978 to designs by Charles Moore with Perez Architects. The idea came in the early 1970s from leaders of the local Italian-American community, who wanted a lasting public tribute to the city's Italian immigrants. Moore's answer was a fountain shaped like the Italian peninsula, ringed by curved colonnades, with a clock tower, a bell tower and a Roman temple, the last two drawn as abstract space frames. Classical orders are handled playfully in stainless steel and neon, and water jets stand in for Corinthian acanthus leaves. Praised at its opening, the plaza soon decayed, as the buildings meant to surround it never came. It was fully restored by 2004, as the Lykes Center next door became a hotel.

Football is the main sport at the Sapporo Dome, a stadium in Sapporo on the Japanese island of Hokkaido that opened in 2001 with room for 41,580. Hiroshi Hara's design gives it two completely different playing surfaces. Baseball is played on artificial turf laid below; for football, a grass pitch is slid into the stadium and back out when needed. Switching from baseball to football starts with putting the turf away. Sliding pitches are also found at stadiums in the Netherlands, Germany and the United States. It became the first venue at world championship or Winter Olympic level to stage skiing both indoors and at night, with cross-country sprints and the cross-country leg of a Nordic combined sprint; the same hovering system that moves the turf helped make the snow.

High in the Arctic, on Spitsbergen, a Norwegian island in the Svalbard archipelago, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault keeps a safe backup of the planet's crop diversity. Peter W. Soderman designed it. Gene banks around the world send copies of their seeds here for long-term storage. The vault lies 130 metres into a sandstone mountain and is guarded by strong security systems. The first seeds came in January 2008, and the official opening followed on 26 February. Mirrors, prisms and reflective stainless steel fill the roof and entrance. Along the roof and down the front runs a lit artwork, Perpetual Repercussion by Dyveke Sanne, which marks the vault from afar. In October 2016, warmth and heavy rain pushed far more water into the entrance, but the design made it freeze several metres in, so the seeds were never at risk.

Steel bars arranged as a vertical lattice hyperboloid make up the Adziogol Lighthouse, one of only two such towers still in service as lighthouses in Ukraine's Dnieper Estuary. Vladimir Shukhov designed it in 1910 and built it in 1911. Its base is a concrete pier set on a very small island in the joint Dnieper-Bug Estuary, about 2.5 km north of Rybalche village, and its name comes from the Cape of Adzhyhol, which lies to the north. Only a boat can get you there. Paired with a front light, the Stanislav Range Front Light, it acts as a range light, showing ships the way into the Dnieper or the Southern Buh River. A Russian missile strike on 22 July 2022 damaged the tower, with three rockets hitting it.

Renzo Piano designed the Modern Wing, which opened on 16 May 2009 as the biggest addition the Art Institute of Chicago had ever made, growing the museum's footprint to almost one million square feet. The wing holds the museum's European art from the early 20th century, among it The Old Guitarist by Picasso, Bathers by a River by Matisse and Time Transfixed by Magritte. Screens on the windows keep direct sun off the art, and a gallery Piano designed alongside the wing uses the same screens. In 2009 it won at the Chicago Innovation Awards. Even though tickets rose in price by a quarter, the wing did much to draw more visitors. A year after it opened, the museum sued the engineers Ove Arup for $10 million, claiming faults in the concrete floors and the air-circulation systems.

Built to house athletes at the 1982 Asian Games, the Asian Games Village in New Delhi was designed by Raj Rewal. It occupies the ruins of Siri Fort, raised by the Khalji dynasty in the 15th century. There are 700 homes in all: 200 separate houses and 500 flats, in buildings two to four storeys tall. Courtyards are arranged in a hierarchy that runs through the complex at several levels. The streets are kept narrow and shady and split into short stretches, giving pauses, places to rest and turning points. Terraces give partly private space and call to mind the houses of Jaisalmer. Cars and people on foot have separate routes that still connect closely: roads around the edge feed dead-end parking courts, and from these residents reach the garages or car porches attached to their homes.

Part of the Central University of Venezuela in Caracas, the Aula Magna is an auditorium that Carlos Raúl Villanueva designed in the 1940s. The Danish firm Christiani & Nielsen had just four months to build it, under a contract running from 28 November 1952 to 31 March 1953. The hall was the centrepiece of the Synthesis of the Arts, Villanueva's plan to create and redesign the campus. He called his buildings 'movements' rather than objects, and this was number four. What stands out most is the set of acoustic 'clouds', Alexander Calder's Floating Clouds of 1953, which join art and technology and serve looks as well as practical needs. At first they were not meant to go inside the hall. In November 2000, UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site because of its value as art and as architecture.

Also called Le Palais Hindou, the Hindu Palace, the Baron Empain Palace is a historic mansion in Heliopolis, north-east of central Cairo. Baron Édouard Empain arrived in Egypt in 1904, aiming to grow his business empire and lay railway lines. By 1906 he had taken on the architect Ernest Jaspar to help shape a 'Heliopolis style' for the new district. The palace itself was the work of a French architect, Alexandre Marcel. Drawing mainly on Angkor Wat in Cambodia and on Orissa's Hindu temples in India, it rose from 1907 to 1911 in reinforced concrete, at that time a mark of luxury. After the Baron's death in 1929, and Egypt's revolution of 1952, the house stood empty. A 2012 agreement with the Belgian government set out to restore it jointly as an international centre for art and culture.

On the northern edge of Copenhagen, in Klampenborg, the Bellevue Theatre opened in 1936 as a fashionable, or mondain, summer theatre. Arne Jacobsen set up his own practice in 1930, and soon after, early in that decade, he won a competition to masterplan the Bellevue area of Klampenborg in Gentofte Municipality. The theatre counts among his most important buildings and is held up as a model of early Danish functionalism. Canvas and bamboo line the walls, the balcony and the proscenium. Since it opened again as a theatre, its programme has leaned heavily towards modern music, with rock musicals above all.

Every year the Busan International Film Festival uses the Busan Cinema Center as its official home, in the Centum City district of Busan, South Korea. Its other name, Dureraum, means roughly 'enjoying seeing movies together'. Coop Himmelb(l)au designed it, and it dates from 2011; in 2007 the design took the Chicago Athenaeum's International Architecture Award. The centre is made up of three buildings, named Cine Mountain, Biff Hill and Double Cone. Next to them are the open-air Biff Theater, sheltered by the Small Roof, and Dureraum Square, which sits beneath the Big Roof. Both roofs are made of steel, and Guinness World Records has certified the Big Roof as the longest cantilevered roof anywhere.

Bulgaria's communist government built the Buzludzha Monument, officially the Monument House of the Bulgarian Communist Party, on Buzludzha Peak in the centre of the country, and opened it in 1981. Work started on 23 January 1974, led by the architect Georgi Stoilov. To give it firm footing, the summit was blasted flat with TNT, cutting the peak from 1,441 to 1,432 metres. The building is an example of the futurist style found in many communist state buildings. Inside, about 937 square metres of mosaics, made from 35 tons of cobalt glass, tell the party's history, and a red star-shaped window used to crown the hall. Upkeep stopped altogether in 1989, and because the structure has weakened, visitors are kept out. Europa Nostra listed it in 2018 among the seven heritage sites in Europe most at risk.

Lisbon's Calouste Gulbenkian Museum, dating from 1969, holds a private art collection ranked among the most important in the world. Three architects, Pedro Cid, Ruy Jervis d'Athouguia and Alberto J. Pessoa, won the design as a team, while the park around it was laid out by the landscape architects Gonçalo Ribeiro Telles and António Viana Barreto. The building was conceived from the start to display the collection. That was fairly rare then, since most museums occupied buildings first put up for some other use. The permanent galleries follow both date and geography, splitting the visit into two separate routes. The first route features Greek and Roman art from classical antiquity, with work from the Nile Valley and the ancient Near East. The building was awarded the Valmor Prize in 1975.

Chichu means 'in the earth', and Tadao Ando's art museum of 2004 is set straight into the southern end of Naoshima, an island in Japan's Kagawa Prefecture. Though it lies below ground, the design lets daylight alone light several of the works, so they look different as the day goes on, and the building itself becomes part of the same world as the art. James Turrell and Walter De Maria have permanent installations here, and there are paintings from Claude Monet's Water Lilies series. Monet loved gardening, so the garden and ponds outside were planned from his own garden designs and his paintings, and they even grow water lilies of the kinds he painted. The museum is run by the Fukutake Foundation, which the Benesse Corporation set up as one of its projects.

Richard Boyle, 3rd Earl of Burlington, designed and built Chiswick House, a Neo-Palladian villa in the London district of Chiswick, and finished it in 1729. A journey to Italy in 1719 had given him a passion for Palladian architecture. He made the villa big enough for his art collection, said to hold 'some of the best pictures in Europe', and for his best furniture. Before it, a Jacobean house stood on the site. William Kent, an architect and landscape designer, did most of the work on the garden, which is among the first English landscape gardens. The house went downhill in the 19th century, and the Cavendish family rented it out. It is now listed at Grade I and looked after by English Heritage.

I. M. Pei designed the Cleo Rogers Memorial Library in Columbus, Indiana, the lead library of the Bartholomew County Public Library system, and it dates from 1969. Young architects had already given Columbus several modern buildings by the early 1960s through the Cummins Foundation Architectural Program, though this library was not one of them. It takes the form of a brick pavilion, closed by solid walls to the east and west, with its main door set off-centre at the west end. Overhead, a coffered concrete ceiling holds lights in deep square hollows. The Library Plaza in front shares the building's brick and concrete and frames Henry Moore's sculpture Large Arch. All three were placed to answer Eliel Saarinen's First Christian Church and the Irwin House. Until the plaza was built, the city had few civic places for people to gather.

Only graduate students live in Graduate House, a University of Toronto residence by Thom Mayne of Morphosis working with the Toronto firm Teeple Architects. It opened in 2000 and sleeps 435, in flat-style suites with between two and five bedrooms. The building fills the north-east corner where Spadina Avenue crosses Harbord Street, on the west side of the St. George campus. A long arm juts out across half the width of Harbord Street, bearing a huge 'University of Toronto' sign, so the building doubles as the campus's main western gateway. Until 2000, graduate students were housed in the St. George Apartments at 321 Bloor Street West. The residence is seen as one of the more significant buildings by Mayne, who received the Pritzker Prize in 2005.

Owned by the University of Sheffield, the Arts Tower opened in 1965 after four years of building that began in 1961, to designs by Gollins, Melvin, Ward & Partners. Many people believe it took its cue from New York's Seagram Building, which looks alike but is far bigger, or that it is tied to two Manchester buildings, New Century House and the CIS Tower. No written record backs either idea, even if all four plainly share a look. At first, people reached the door across a broad bridge that passed between fountains above a shallow pool. Inside, two standard lifts serve the floors along with a 38-car paternoster, the biggest of the handful still running in Britain. At mezzanine level a bridge joins the tower to the Western Bank Library, and both buildings are listed Grade II*.

Marina Tabassum designed the Bait ur Rouf Mosque, finished in 2012, for a part of Dhaka that is prone to floods. Its land came from Sufia Khatun, a widow who gave part of her plot for a mosque after two of her daughters died. The plan follows an axis set 13 degrees off the Qibla. That let the architect turn the prayer hall to face the right way, and it left light courts on all four sides, with space for other uses. Dozens of round holes, scattered at random through the walls and roof, admit daylight that moves across the interior as light and shadow, deepening its spiritual mood. Handmade terracotta brick walls let air through, keeping the rooms cool even in the heat. In 2016 it was among six winners of the Aga Khan Award for Architecture.

Rising over Fitzrovia in London, the BT Tower was completed in 1964 as a communications tower for the General Post Office. It replaced a lower 1940s steel lattice mast on top of the Museum Telephone Exchange, named for the nearby British Museum. The design came from the Ministry of Public Building and Works, led by Eric Bedford and G R Yeats as chief architects. The glass skin was tinted so the tower would not overheat. The first design called for a height of only 111 metres. The foundations go 53 metres down through London clay to a square concrete raft 27 metres across, strengthened with six layers of cables, with a reinforced concrete pyramid on top. On completion no structure in London stood taller, and it kept that title until 1980. It was listed Grade II in 2003.

Madrid knows this building at Calle del Greco 4 as La Corona de Espinas, the Crown of Thorns. It is home to the Spanish Cultural Heritage Institute (IPCE), a body within the Ministry of Culture that researches, conserves and records the country's cultural heritage. Fernando Higueras and Antonio Miró were the architects, and the building dates from 1970. Built of reinforced concrete, it forms a ring four storeys high, topped by a cornice of sharp, jagged points. It ranks among the most important pieces of contemporary architecture in Spain. On 16 November 2001 it was given protection as a Bien de Interés Cultural, a Heritage Site of Cultural Interest.

Oslo's municipal library, which is also Norway's first and biggest, runs Deichman Bjørvika as one of its buildings. The library first opened on 12 January 1785, thanks to an endowment from Carl Deichman, whose bequest of 7,000 books and 150 manuscripts became the core of its holdings. Two practices, Lundhagem and Atelier Oslo, designed the Bjørvika building, and the public came in for the first time on 18 June 2020. Among the prizes it has collected is the IFLA/Systematic Public Library of the Year award. Manuscripts given to the Future Library project are kept here too, including writing by David Mitchell and Margaret Atwood. Anyone registered can come in between 7 in the morning and 10 at night, seven days a week, whether or not staff are on duty.

Queen Alia International Airport sits at Zizya, 30 kilometres south of Amman, Jordan's capital and biggest city. It first opened in 1983, built because traffic had outgrown Amman Civil Airport. Foster + Partners designed new terminals, and once these were inaugurated in 2013 the original ones were pulled down. Bedouin tents gave the idea for the new roof, a field of 127 concrete domes that weigh as much as 600 tonnes each. The old terminal saw its final departure at 10:05 pm on 20 March 2013. Every operation then moved across to the new building, whose own first flight took off at 2:30 am the next day, 21 March 2013.

Pakistan's president both lives and works at Aiwan-e-Sadr in Islamabad, a name that translates as 'President's Palace'. The architect was Edward Durell Stone, who gave it the form of a modern step pyramid. Building work started in 1970 and went on for eleven years. Until it was ready, Pakistan's presidents had lived in Rawalpindi, at the Prince Palace on the Mall. Behind the presidency, beside 4th Avenue, is the President's Colony, a group of homes for the president's staff. So the building is at once the residence and the office of the country's head of state.

Frank Gehry's New World Center, a concert hall from 2011, stands in Miami Beach's South Beach, a block north of Lincoln Road. Beside it lies a 2.5-acre public park by West 8; Gehry gave up that part of the job after the budget was cut. Half an acre of the park is the SoundScape, where people outdoors can watch free live 'wallcasts' of chosen events on a projection wall of 7,000 square feet. Yasuhisa Toyota was responsible for the acoustics. In the atrium, which takes its daylight from the sky above, Gehry's familiar curving shapes take over, above all in a jumbled pile of over thirty rehearsal rooms, offices and recording spaces. It has been called one of his buildings turned inside out, and critics have received it well.

The Borujerdi House in Kashan, Iran, dates from 1857 and today serves as a historic house museum. Its story includes a bride from the wealthy Tabātabāei family; some years before, its architect, Ustad Ali Maryam, had built the nearby Tabatabai House for that same family. Like other traditional Iranian homes, it is divided into a biruni, or public part, and an andaruni, or private quarters, arranged with a courtyard, a fountain pool and an iwan two storeys high. Over the main hall rises a khishkhan, a kind of central dome. The roof carries three windcatchers, each 40 metres tall: one above the entrance area and two above the main hall. Stucco, glass work and ayeneh-kari decorate the house, along with frescoes painted by Kamal-ol-Molk. Students can read both halves of a traditional Iranian house in this one building.

Studio Daniel Libeskind and Davis Partnership Architects designed the Frederic C. Hamilton Building, an extension of the Denver Art Museum, as a joint venture. Clad in titanium and glass, it opened on 7 October 2006, the first of Libeskind's buildings finished in the US. Its pointed forms recall the nearby Rockies and the geometric crystals at their base; Libeskind cited the mountains' light and geology as an inspiration. It holds the museum's Modern and Contemporary, African and Oceanic art. The Duncan Pavilion, added to the Bach Wing, carries bridge traffic from it and from Gio Ponti's 1971 North Building, now the Martin Building. In 2007 its distinctive steel arrangement won an AISC Presidential Award of Excellence, and the American Institute of Architects cited it as a successful example of Building Information Modeling.

The Deutsches Architekturmuseum stands on the Museumsufer in Frankfurt, inside a building from the 18th century. In 1984 Oswald Mathias Ungers remade its interior to a concept he described as 'elemental Platonic buildings within elemental Platonic buildings': pure forms nested inside the old shell. 'From Ancient Huts to Skyscrapers', the permanent display, follows the history of architecture in Germany. Each year the museum also stages several temporary exhibitions and holds conferences, symposia and lectures. Its holdings run to around 180,000 drawings and 600 models, with pieces by Erich Mendelsohn, Mies van der Rohe, Archigram and Frank O. Gehry among them. Students can see here how a new interior order can be set inside an older structure, and how architects draw and model their ideas.

Sean Godsell built Kew House in 1996–1997 as his own family's home, in Kew, Melbourne. A minimalist glass box of 18 by 9 metres, it is enclosed on two sides by rusted metal screens and projects 5.5 metres over a steep slope. Rust, oiled second-hand boards and recycled decking replace 'precious' detail, making a house described as elemental rather than processed. The Japanese-influenced plan has no corridors: space is split only by the kitchen and bathroom, a long central wall holding the fireplace and cupboards, and sliding screens. On the north and west, the screens keep summer sun off the windows, and parts lift to let sunlight warm the living areas on colder days. In 2000 the International Architecture Year Book saw in it a speculation on an Australian vernacular mixing east and west.

Opened on 20 January 2007, the Olympic Sculpture Park in downtown Seattle is a free public park of modern and contemporary sculpture, created and run by the Seattle Art Museum. Weiss/Manfredi Architects led the design, with Charles Anderson Landscape Architecture and Magnusson Klemencic Associates. Unocal, an oil and gas company, used the industrial site until the 1970s; it then lay contaminated as a brownfield until the museum proposed making it one of downtown's few green spaces. The park joins a pavilion indoors, a 9-acre open-air sculpture museum and a beach on Puget Sound. Along the shore, 50,000 tonnes of riprap form a three-level underwater slope. Permanent sculptures, temporary works and site-specific installations sit side by side, but the salt water has corroded pieces made mostly of bare wood and metal. It shows a polluted industrial edge turned into public landscape.

The centre of Tel Aviv's municipal government is Tel Aviv City Hall, a Brutalist building that architect Menachem Cohen designed in the 1950s. At first the municipality had its offices on Rothschild Boulevard, and in 1972 the old Skora building became a museum of the city's history. Below the new building spreads a large plaza, laid out as a central place for public events and ceremonies. Its first name was Kings of Israel Square. In 1995 Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated there, and the square was renamed Rabin Square after him. On many occasions the building has been used to express solidarity with other countries after disasters and terrorist attacks. For students, it pairs a Brutalist civic block with the public square laid out at its base.

The Royal Institute of British Architects has its headquarters at 66 Portland Place, an office building in the Marylebone district of central London. From 1859 the institute had been based at 9 Conduit Street. The competition for the new building drew 284 entries, many for such a modest construction, though perhaps to be expected given what it would house; the design is George Grey Wornum's. King George V and Queen Mary opened it officially on 8 November 1934. The style is chiefly Art Deco mixed with late neoclassical, also named Imperial Neoclassical after Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker. On the outside, Deco shows in the bronze doors, the architectural motifs and a main window spanning more than one storey. The building gained grade II* listing on 14 September 1970, 37 years after it was built.

Completed in 1998, Aula Magna is Stockholm University's biggest auditorium. Its architect, Ralph Erskine, also designed several neighbouring university buildings: Allhuset, the Stockholm University Library, Aktiverum (Frescatihallen) and the House of Laws. Aula Magna is set into the ground, and Erskine split its facade into many volumes that vary in size, structure and height. The roof can be seen from far away; its sun reflectors, a feature typical of Erskine, bring daylight down into the auditorium through skylights. In the lower foyer the bedrock is left exposed, which gives the interior a natural feel. The auditorium's design drew on the semi-circular plan of an ancient amphitheatre. It is a good case of bringing daylight into a large hall from above, within a group of university buildings by the same architect.

Ernst von Ihne designed the Bode Museum, a listed 1904 building on Berlin's Museum Island, in the city's historic centre. It first bore the name Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum, honouring Emperor Frederick III; in 1956 it was renamed for Wilhelm von Bode, its first curator. During the Second World War, some of the collection was kept safe in an anti-aircraft tower, the Flakturm Friedrichshain. Closed for repairs in 1997, it reopened on 18 October 2006 after a €156 million refurbishment. Bode believed in mixing art collections, and in that spirit the museum now shows sculpture and Byzantine art alongside coins and medals. In 1999 UNESCO added Museum Island, this building included, to its World Heritage List, for outstanding architecture and as a record of how museums grew into a cultural phenomenon between the late 19th century and the early 20th.

Giovanni Michelucci drew up the plans for the church of San Giovanni Battista, built from 1960 to 1963 in Campi Bisenzio, near Florence. It stands in a large rest area shared by two autostrade, the Italian motorways. Formally dedicated to John the Baptist, it also became known as the Church of the Freeway of the Sun, because it lies between the Autostrada del Sole and the A11 Firenze-Mare highway. The design aims to reflect church designs both modern and traditional. Its walls are of stone and concrete; the copper roof has turned green from oxidation on the outside, while inside it is burnished blond. Sinuous curves shape the asymmetrical plan and give a sense of fluid space. Students can see how one building aims to hold modern and traditional church design, and how its materials read differently outside and in.

Powell & Moya's Churchill Gardens, finished in 1962, is a large Pimlico housing estate in Westminster, London. Its 32 blocks hold 1,600 homes, and it is the only housing scheme carried through under the Abercrombie Plan, which aimed to rebuild London along more 'efficient' lines. A pioneering case of mixed development, it served as a model for many later public housing schemes; few of them reached its scale, and fewer still its architectural distinction or social mix. In many of the taller blocks, lifts open directly onto the street: a local lift stops at every floor, while an express lift calls only at every third floor. The estate also has the Pimlico District Heating Undertaking, an early and rare case of district heating in Britain. Its landscape is listed Grade II on the Register of Historic Parks and Gardens.

Santiago Calatrava and Félix Candela designed Valencia's City of Arts and Sciences, a complex for culture and architecture. It occupies the southeastern end of the old Turia riverbed; the river was drained and diverted after a disastrous flood in 1957. Work started in July 1996, and the complex opened officially on 16 April 1998 with L'Hemisfèric. That building, about 13,000 m² in surface, is meant to look like a giant eye whose eyelid opens onto the water pool around it. The lid is made of long aluminium awnings that fold up together into a brise-soleil roof, opening along the eye's curved axis. L'Umbracle (2001) is an open structure wrapped around a landscaped walk with plants native to Valencia. The 1991 budget was €300 million for three structures; more were added, which helped the cost rise threefold.

The Des Moines Art Center grew in three stages, each by a different architect, which lets students compare three approaches on one site. Construction started in 1945, and Eliel Saarinen's original wing, combining Art Nouveau and Art Deco styles, opened in 1948. I. M. Pei added a second wing in a Modernist style, designed in 1966 for large-scale sculpture and completed in 1968. Richard Meier's third wing followed in 1985, designed to let in as much natural ambient light as possible. The museum holds an extensive collection of paintings, sculpture, modern art and mixed media, and since 2009 it has also run the Pappajohn Sculpture Park in Western Gateway Park downtown. Seen together, the three wings trace the museum's growth from its opening to the mid-1980s.

Product, industrial, graphic, fashion and architectural design are all shown at the Design Museum in Kensington, London. Its first home was a banana warehouse from the 1940s at Shad Thames, on the Thames's south bank. In 2016, helped by a £17.5 million gift from Sir Terence Conran, it moved into the old Commonwealth Institute: a Grade II* listed landmark of the 1960s by Robert Matthew, Johnson-Marshall and Partners, empty for more than ten years before a team led by John Pawson developed it. The museum opened in Kensington on 24 November 2016. A main staircase rises from the atrium to every floor, with views up to the hyperbolic paraboloid roof. Under that roof, the top floor houses Designer Maker User, a permanent display of key objects from the collection. It shows a listed modern building given a new use.

In Beitou Park, within Taipei's Beitou District, the Beitou branch of the Taipei Public Library opened in November 2006. Bio-architecture Formosana designed the two-storey building as an eco-friendly green building, intended to curb its consumption of water and electricity. Large windows bring in daylight and reduce the electricity needed for lighting. The roof does two jobs. It is partly covered with photovoltaic cells that generate electricity, and it captures rainwater, which is stored and then used to flush the toilets. For students, the library is a two-storey public building in which the energy and water strategy is the central design idea, and each measure is tied to a single, visible part of the building: the windows for light, the roof for power and water.

Berthold Lubetkin of Tecton designed Bevin Court, a housing scheme in Finsbury, London, finished in 1954 with Francis Skinner and Douglas Carr Bailey. It stands in Cruikshank Street, on the site of Holford Square, which bombing had destroyed. Taken together, the buildings show Lubetkin's regard for the existing city fabric around them, which sets his work apart from that of many modernists of his generation. After the war, austerity meant a much tighter budget than at Spa Green Estate, Tecton's housing showpiece, and Lubetkin had to drop amenities he had planned: no balconies, no community centre, no nursery school. He put his effort into the social space instead. The building was listed grade II* in December 1998, and the London Borough of Islington restored it in 2014–2016.

Muryangsujeon is the main hall of Buseoksa, a Buddhist temple close to Bonghwangsan mountain, in the Buseok-myeon area of Yeongju, South Korea. Rebuilt in 1376, it ranks as the country's second-oldest wooden building still standing, and it is one of the few buildings left from the Goryeo era. Set on the temple's highest level, the hall enshrines Amitabha. According to stained paper discovered in 1916, the hall had been rebuilt in the first years of Goryeo, and in 1358 an enemy set it on fire. The temple sits on a steep mountain, and in Korea the skill of bringing building and nature into harmony is seen as the core of architecture. For students, it is a rare surviving precedent of early Korean timber construction, set on a steep slope.

Castello di Rivoli, in the Metropolitan City of Turin, was once a residence of the Royal House of Savoy. Its origins probably go back to the 9th or 10th century. In 1716 the architect Filippo Juvarra stepped in with a grand plan, which was never finished. Heavy damage in the Second World War left the building mostly abandoned until restoration started again in 1979. The first renovation after the war was led by Andrea Bruno, an architect from Turin. Since 1997 it has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List, together with 13 other Savoy residences. For students, it is a layered case: an unfinished grand scheme on a much older castle, restored after decades of neglect and given a new use.

Tomás Sanabria's Hotel Humboldt, from 1956, sits on top of Cerro Ávila in Caracas, at 2,140 metres above sea level. It belonged to a scheme for joining the city to the coast with a complex for tourism and leisure, served by the cable car. A cylindrical tower with views in every direction (360°) is the heart of the design. Its glass and aluminium skin helped warm the building, and tilting windows meant routine cleaning could be done from inside. Restoration was later led by Gregory Vertullo, a Venezuelan architect who specialises in restoring architectural monuments, working with professionals from Venezuela and abroad; the adjoining Salón Boîte was returned fully to its original wall-covering patterns and carpet colour. The hotel is a case of a building conceived together with transport infrastructure to open a mountain summit to visitors.

In mid-1911, aged 31, Josef Gočár designed the House of the Black Madonna in Prague's Old Town for František Josef Herbst, a wholesale merchant. The cubist building was finished in 1912 and takes its name from a baroque Black Madonna sculpture that decorates it, left over from an earlier building on the site. Its prominent spot in the city centre meant strict rules on harmony: the department store must not clash with its historic surroundings. A frame of reinforced concrete made large interiors possible without ceiling supports, better suited to Cubist aesthetics. Years of alterations had damaged its original fabric before a full restoration in 2003. It shows how a new style can work within rules set by a historic city centre.

Oscar Niemeyer designed the Iate Tênis Clube, a recreational club beside Lake Pampulha in Belo Horizonte. Its original name was Iate Golfe Clube. In the early 1940s, when a dam was creating the lake, Juscelino Kubitschek, then mayor of the state capital of Minas Gerais, commissioned four Niemeyer buildings, and this is one of them. The club's main architectural feature is a building whose upper floor holds the Portinari Room, named for Candido Portinari, who painted one of the murals there. Roberto Burle Marx laid out the gardens in its outdoor areas. A party hall and gym were added in an annex in the 1970s. UNESCO named the Architectural Ensemble of Pampulha a World Heritage Site in 2016, so the club is best studied together with its three companion buildings.

In Shirakawa Park, in Naka-ku, Nagoya, Kisho Kurokawa's Nagoya City Art Museum occupies a long, triangular plot ringed by trees. Its origins lie in the Nagoya City Basic Plan of 1977, which proposed an art museum for the city; the building itself dates from 1987. Its galleries are underground, and a sunken garden lets daylight into the route that leads down to them. Two axes order the plan: a main one running north–south and a second one that opens toward the northwest. The museum says the design also draws on traditional Japanese forms and local motifs. It is a useful study in bringing daylight to underground galleries and in setting a museum on a tree-lined park site.

Standing 52 storeys and 197.7 metres (649 feet) tall, OCBC Centre in Singapore is the current headquarters of OCBC Bank. The American architect I. M. Pei designed it, and it is a prominent case of Brutalism, a style popular in the 1960s and 1970s. The tower was formally inaugurated on 1 October 1976; it was then the second-tallest building in both Singapore and South East Asia. For students, it is a clear example of Pei working in the Brutalist idiom, and of a 1970s bank headquarters tower in South East Asia.

André Aubert, Marcel Dastugue and Paul Viard designed the Palais de Tokyo, which houses modern and contemporary art on avenue du Président-Wilson (number 13), across from the Trocadéro in Paris's 16th arrondissement. Between it and the Seine runs the Avenue de New-York, a street known from 1918 to 1945 as Avenue de Tokio. President Lebrun opened the building on 24 May 1937, during that year's International Exposition of Art and Technology in Modern Life. The French state owns the western wing; since March 2002 it has housed the Site de création contemporaine, France's largest museum for temporary shows of contemporary art. Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal remodelled and enlarged it in 2012 and later went on to win the Pritzker Prize.

Covering 55.5 hectares, the parc de la Villette ranks third in size among the parks of Paris and lies at the city's northeastern edge, in the 19th arrondissement. Bernard Tschumi, a French architect with Swiss roots, won a major competition for it in 1982–83 within François Mitterrand's Grands Projets, consulting the philosopher Jacques Derrida as he prepared his entry. With Colin Fournier he built it between 1984 and 1987, where the city's vast abattoirs and the national wholesale meat market once stood. The park is intended to draw on deconstructivist ideas. Its follies, themed gardens and open spaces share the grounds with museums, concert halls and theatres that well-known contemporary architects, Christian de Portzamparc among them, have designed since it was created. For students, it is a built test of deconstructivist ideas at the scale of a city park.

Paul Löbe House, in the government district of Berlin, holds offices for the German Bundestag. An urban design competition for the Spreebogen area was announced in 1992; a second competition, begun in autumn 1994 to carry the project out, was won by Stephan Braunfels of Munich with a design for both the Paul Löbe House and the Marie-Elisabeth Lüders House. Their architecture binds the pair together: the edges of their roofs follow the line of the Spree, and two bridges link the buildings across the river. This east–west link stands for a united East and West Germany, where the Berlin Wall once crossed the built-up area, and cancels out the Nazi-era plan for a 'world capital Germania', expressed here as a north–south axis. A spacious central hall cuts through the whole building, and the side courtyards hold art-in-architecture works.

Berlin's Tempodrom, sometimes called the Neues Tempodrom, is a venue for many kinds of events. Irene Moessinger founded it, and in 1980 it opened inside a big circus tent beside the Berlin Wall, on the western side of Potsdamer Platz. Not until 2001 did it get a permanent home, built where the old Anhalter Bahnhof had stood; the station's war-damaged ruins had been cleared in 1960. Von Gerkan, Marg und Partner (gmp) were engaged to design the new building. It has two arenas, both round. Over the larger one, at the centre, spans a 37-metre roof of steel and concrete panels, meant to recall the shape of the tents on the original site. For students, it is a clear case of a permanent building carrying the memory of a temporary one, on a site with its own layered history.

Astley Castle, in North Warwickshire, is a ruined, moated and fortified 16th-century manor house. The Greys rebuilt it in 1555, and most of what survives is from then or after. Badly damaged by fire in 1978 while serving as a hotel, it lay derelict and neglected, officially a Building at Risk. Its owners began planning a restoration in the early 2000s with English Heritage, the Landmark Trust and the local authority. Witherford Watson Mann Architects, with the engineers Mann Williams and Price & Myers, inserted modern elements into the largely Renaissance remains, and in 2012 it reopened as a holiday let. In 2013 it won the RIBA Stirling Prize, cited as an 'exceptional example' of joining an ancient monument to modern architecture. It is a strong precedent for any student working on new design inside a ruin.

Karl Schwanzer designed Munich's BMW Headquarters, known as the BMW Tower and in German as the 'BMW four-cylinder', along with the BMW Museum. The high-rise stands in the Am Riesenfeld area; work ran from 1968 to 1972, finishing in time for that year's Summer Olympics. Tower and museum together are meant to suggest a car engine: the tower as four cylinders, the museum as the cylinder head. The four upright cylinders sit side by side and opposite one another. They do not rest on the ground but hang from a central support tower. While it was being built, each floor was put together at ground level and then lifted into place. It is a clear example of a suspended structure in a high-rise.

Arata Isozaki designed Casals Hall, a concert hall in Ochanomizu, Tokyo. Built for chamber music, it opened in 1987 with a shoebox-type auditorium of 511 seats. Ten years later, in 1997, an organ by Jürgen Ahrend with 41 stops was added to mark the anniversary. The hall was first owned and sponsored by the publisher Shufunotomo Company, but economic conditions brought that funding to an end in 2000. For students, it is a compact study of the shoebox model for chamber music, and a reminder of how much a cultural building depends on lasting support.

The Centro Cultural São Paulo, a public institution, answers to the city's Municipal Department of Culture. It gathers the Pinacoteca Municipal, the record collection named after Oneyda Alvarenga and the holdings of the Folklore Research Mission of Mário de Andrade, as well as theatres, a cinema, exhibition spaces, libraries and a space for courses. It is seen as one of São Paulo's first 'cultural centres' in the strict sense. After competitive bidding, the city hired the architects Eurico Prado Lopes and Luiz Benedito de Castro Telles for a new library on part of the 300,000 m² left by the abandoned Nova Vergueiro project, north of Vergueiro metro station. Rather than only enlarging the existing library named after Mário de Andrade, the scheme was reworked with the Centre Pompidou as its model, which makes the two a useful pairing for students.

Frank Gehry's DZ Bank Building, once called the DG Bank Building, stands on Berlin's Pariser Platz, at number 3. It combines three uses in one building: offices, conference space and residences. Building work started in 1998 and ended in 2000. Over part of it sits a refined glass-grid roof, shaped into a complex curve of the kind typical of Gehry's work. For students, the building shows how offices, conference rooms and homes can share one address, and how a complex curved roof can be built as a grid of glass.

Until the FOCSA went up in 1956, no residential building in Cuba was taller than Havana's Edificio López Serrano. Ricardo Mira designed it in 1929. Its construction was backed by José Antonio López Serrano, the publisher behind La Moderna Poesía, and in 1941 Mira designed the Obispo Street bookstore of La Moderna Poesía for him too. It is often likened to the Bacardi Building in Old Havana, finished two years earlier, because the two share a similar massing and a central tower. The frame is structural steel to U.S. standards. Over the ten storeys of the main block, a central tower of four apartments stands on ten steel columns that project from the main mass. Its outer walls are brick, finished with one inch of integral-colour cement plaster. It shows a steel-framed Art Deco apartment block with a central tower.

Better known as the Hung Hom Coliseum, the Hong Kong Coliseum is an indoor arena for many uses on Hung Hom Bay in Kowloon, close to Hung Hom station. It was built by the Urban Council and opened officially on 27 April 1983. Its main designer is considered to be Pau Shiu-hung, once Director of Architectural Services for the HKSAR Government. Seats surround the rectangular arena floor on all four sides, with the top and most distant rows reaching 41 metres up. For shows, the floor can be laid with different coverings, such as removable wooden flooring or rubber roll-outs of several kinds. For students, it is a compact study in how seating on all four sides of a flexible floor can serve many uses.

On Kyoto's western outskirts, the Katsura Imperial Villa is an Imperial residence together with its gardens and outbuildings, linked to Prince Toshihito and Toshitada. At first the palace was owned by the Hachijō-no-miya family's prince. He lacked wealth and resources, so the first villa was a modest building, compared to 'a teahouse in the melon patch'. The mats at Katsura generate the sprawling, pinwheel-shaped plan the villa has now. Its shoji, white translucent screens stiffened with a wooden lattice, may be fixed, hanging or sliding. Both the main villa and the teahouses for the tea ceremony set in the strolling gardens are placed to make the most of varied foliage and views that change with the seasons. The grounds count as a notable example of traditional Japanese gardening, and the villa is a precedent for planning from the mat.

Nicknamed The Boiled Egg, Paul Andreu's National Centre for the Performing Arts in Xicheng, Beijing, is an arts centre with an opera house, dating from 2007. A shell of structural steel forms its exterior. Within are an opera hall, a music hall, a theatre and halls for art exhibitions, plus restaurants, audio shops and other support facilities. Its central section is an involute glass curtain wall of over 1,200 panes of ultra-white glass. Groundwater was a problem: engineers and technicians answered it by pouring a concrete wall underground, running from the groundwater's highest level down to a clay layer 60 metres below the surface. Responding to critics, Andreu argued that ancient Chinese architecture does have value, but that Beijing, as the national capital and an important international city, also needs modern architecture.

Minoru Yamasaki designed One Woodward Avenue in 1962 as the new headquarters of the Michigan Consolidated Gas Company, whose name the 28-storey office tower in downtown Detroit first carried. The tower itself stands on a raised base that hides its loading dock and service entrances. From that base, the lobby rises two storeys inside walls of chrome-framed glass panels, set back from the facade so that a loggia runs round all four sides. In the 1980s it was renamed the American Natural Resources Building. In December 2012 Dan Gilbert announced that his company, Rock Ventures, had bought the tower and that Quicken Loans would take eight of its floors. It is a compact study in raising an office tower on a platform above its services.

Two 36-storey towers make up Pennzoil Place in Downtown Houston. Philip Johnson/John Burgee Architects designed them, working from an idea by Eli Attia, a staff architect there; Gerald D. Hines Interests developed the project. Both towers are trapezoidal and 151 metres high, set ten feet apart and clad in aluminium and dark bronze glass. A pyramid-shaped glass atrium 35 metres tall encloses the entire street-level plaza between them. The pair was deliberately planned as an optical illusion, so it looks different depending on where you stand. In architectural circles it is seen as significant for breaking with the modernist glass box popularised by Mies van der Rohe's followers and for opening the era of postmodernism. In 1975 Ada Louise Huxtable, The New York Times critic, called it 'Building of the Decade' for the dramatic silhouette it gave the Houston skyline.

Venezia Santa Lucia is the main railway station of Venice, in north-eastern Italy. The Ponte degli Scalzi, a bridge over the Grand Canal, connects the concourse in front of it to the sestiere of Santa Croce. Work on a station here began in 1860, under the Austrian Empire. Today's building grew out of a sequence of plans that Angiolo Mazzoni, a rationalist architect, began in 1924 and worked on for the following ten years. Virgilio Vallot won a 1934 contest for the detailed design of the current station, but it was finished in 1952 to a design developed by a different architect, Paul Perilli. Venetian lions adorn both flanks of the facade. For students, the station shows how one building can pass through several architects and decades of planning before it is finished.

Toyo Ito, the Japanese architect, designed VivoCity, a shopping mall in Singapore's HarbourFront precinct, in Bukit Merah. The name comes from the word vivacity. It occupies the former site of the Expo Gateway and Harbour Pavilion, exhibition halls of what was the World Trade Centre and is now the HarbourFront Centre. In 2006 it was topped out on 18 April, soft-launched on 7 October and officially opened on 1 December. A few weeks later its rooftop amphitheatre staged the 2007 Countdown, which ran from 31 December 2006 into 1 January 2007, with homegrown performers of Mediacorp's Channel 5 and 8 and the Top 11 finalists from season two of Singapore Idol. For students, it shows a retail building with a rooftop amphitheatre that has served as a public stage.

Often called Rowley Way, the Alexandra Road Estate is a housing estate in Camden, London. Neave Brown of the council's architects department designed it in 1968 in a brutalist manner, using reinforced concrete cast on site, board-marked, white and unpainted. Three parallel east–west blocks fill a crescent-shaped site with the West Coast Main Line to the north, and controlling train noise and vibration was a major factor in the layout. The eight-storey block beside the railway is a ziggurat that serves as a sound barrier, on foundations set on rubber pads that remove vibration. Its stepped elevation gives each home a private outdoor space on a flat roof. A school, a community centre and parkland sit alongside the 520 flats. In 1993 it became the first post-war council estate to be listed, at Grade II*.

East of Montpellier's city centre, between the old centre and the river Lez, lies Antigone, a district of the French city. The Spanish architect Ricardo Bofill and his Taller de Arquitectura were its architects: Bofill produced the master plan and designed most of the buildings. It stands on land that once held the Joffre Barracks, whose only surviving part is Montpellier's citadel. Most of its buildings are low-income housing, public facilities and neighbourhood shops. For students, it is a whole district planned and largely built by one architect and his studio, with housing, public facilities and shops laid out between a historic centre and a river.

Rising 82 storeys in Lakeshore East, Chicago, Aqua is a mixed-use skyscraper on what used to be a rail yard next to the Chicago River and Lake Michigan. Studio Gang Architects, headed by founder Jeanne Gang, designed it; it was the practice's first skyscraper, and when finished no taller building in the world had been designed by a woman. The facade has a wave-like form, and Gang says the layered limestone outcrops of the Great Lakes region inspired its slabs. Balconies were shaped to keep summer sun off the apartments, cutting the air-conditioning load. Concrete superintendent Paul Treacy was nominated among Engineering News-Record's top 25 newsmakers of 2008 for the exterior formwork that shaped the undulating facade. In 2009 Aqua received the Emporis Skyscraper Award as skyscraper of the year, and in 2010 it made the International Highrise Award shortlist.

In Sydney's central business district, Australia Square Tower holds offices and shops. Conceived in 1961, it got its final design from Harry Seidler & Associates in 1964, after work with the structural engineer Pier Luigi Nervi. On the Pitt Street side stands the Plaza Building, a fairly plain 13-storey rectangular office block finished in 1964. The tower followed in 1967; until 1976 no building in Sydney was taller, and it was then the world's tallest lightweight concrete building. Its round plan, with a setback from the street, let Seidler reduce what he called 'the dark canyon effect'. Twenty vertical columns project from the tower and taper towards the top, carrying radial support beams combined with interlocking ribbed reinforcement. Lendlease owned it first and sold it to GPT in 1981; GPT and Dexus now own it jointly.
